00 — Why Golmet exists

Every software project starts with good intentions: someone writes the requirements, someone draws the architecture, the team aligns the scope. Then the deadline tightens. The requirement changes in a hallway conversation and nobody updates the document. The spec drawn in Figma ends up two sprints behind what the code does. Three months later, the documentation is a museum of things that are no longer true — and the team stops looking at it.

The operator, owner of MinhaOrganizacao, lived this in every project. The company's scheduling product, MeuApp, had requirements in a Word file, decisions scattered across chat messages, and a codebase that grew without anyone knowing exactly which business rules were implemented. When a client asked "why does slot confirmation work like this?", the answer lived in one person's head — and people go on vacation, change companies, forget.

The problem is not a lack of will to document. It's that documenting never wins: while the doc is an effort separate from the code, it always loses priority, and while it is never verified, it always rots. Beautiful documentation tools don't fix that — they just change where the museum lives.

What changes with Golmet

Golmet attacks both sides at once:

Documentation becomes machine-verified. The kit defines a contract (the FORMAT v1): each business rule is a document section with state and owner, and each rule carries evidence — the file, the line and the hash of the code that implements it. golmet validate checks all of it on every run. Stale documentation isn't "annoying", it's a finding that blocks the merge.

The AI does the work nobody had time for. Golmet is not just the validator: it ships with a workflow of skills (gm-*) your AI executes inside the editor. The AI runs the elicitation with the product owner, the AI writes the technical spec from the rules, the AI reviews the code against the spec before the merge. Writing documentation stops being a heroic end-of-sprint effort and becomes a byproduct of development itself.

In practice, with Golmet installed and Opencode open in the workspace:

  • you describe the requirement in plain language and the gm-clarify/gm-req skill turns it into a requirement section with score, state and owner;
  • from the requirement, gm-taskspec generates the functional and technical analysis, and the delivery is born with its tasks;
  • when the code ships, gm-dev-qa runs the suite and golmet validate checks the congruence — whatever diverged shows up with remediation.

The result the operator saw on MeuApp: when the client asks why slot confirmation works like that, the answer is a requirement section with evidence pointing at the code — and it is correct because the machine confirms it on every validation.
